draft.title: Sleep across the lifespan
card: Total sleep time falls as people age. Newborns sleep about 14 to 17 hours a day, teenagers about 8 to 10, and older adults often 6 to 7.
The share of sleep spent in REM also falls. Infants spend about half their sleep in REM. Adults spend about a fifth, and older adults a little less.
In adolescence, the sleep-wake cycle shifts later. Teenagers tend to feel sleepy later at night and want to wake later in the morning.
Early school start times can clash with this shift. A teenager may then get less sleep than their body needs.
draft.remember: With age, total sleep and the share of REM fall. Teenagers' sleep timing moves later.

a.q: Which change in sleep is typical as a person moves from infancy to old age?
opts: Total sleep and the share of REM sleep both fall
Total sleep falls but the share of REM sleep rises
Total sleep rises but the share of REM sleep falls
Total sleep and the share of REM sleep both rise
a.why: Both total sleep and the share of REM fall across the lifespan. The option with REM rising is tempting because adults often talk about dreaming a lot, but infants have the highest share of REM.
a.clue: Infants have the most of both.

b.q: Jai, 16, lives in Ballarat. He feels wide awake at 10 pm and struggles to get up for a 7:30 am school start. What best explains this?
opts: His sleep timing has shifted later, as is common in teens
His share of REM sleep has risen, as is common in teens
His total sleep need has risen above that of infants
His sleep-wake cycle has become shorter than 24 hours
b.why: Adolescents' sleep timing tends to shift later, so Jai feels alert at night and sleepy in the morning. A rising share of REM is wrong, because the REM share falls from infancy onwards.
b.clue: Think about when teenagers tend to feel sleepy.

a.best: Total sleep and the share of REM sleep both fall
